name: Classic Tales
lines: Alice in Wonderland
Faerie, at the Mad Hatter's tea table
The Hatter's teacup
Alice, a curious, polite and brave girl of about seven who fell down the rabbit-hole
Oh! Are you late too? Everyone here seems to be in such a hurry, and nobody will tell me where anything goes.
the Hatter, who keeps it always six o'clock and tea-time, rude, quick and full of riddles he cannot answer
No room! No room! ...Oh, very well, there's plenty of room. Have some wine. There isn't any. Have some tea, then.
the March Hare, mad as a March hare, the Hatter's friend
Take some more tea! You've had none yet, so you can't take less.
the Dormouse, very sleepy, who tells a story about three sisters living at the bottom of a treacle-well
the White Rabbit, nervous, with a waistcoat and a pocket-watch, always late for the Duchess
Oh my ears and whiskers, how late it's getting! The Duchess! She'll get me executed!
the Cheshire Cat, who grins, talks in puzzles and vanishes slowly, ending with the grin
We're all mad here. I'm mad. You're mad. You must be, or you wouldn't have come here.
The Queen of Hearts
the Queen of Hearts, the furious queen of the playing cards who shouts 'Off with their heads!', though nobody is ever actually executed
Can you play croquet? Then join in! The hoops are soldiers and the mallets are flamingos, and if you cheat... OFF WITH YOUR HEAD!
Why is a raven like a writing-desk? ...No, don't answer yet. Sit down. Your hair wants cutting. Now, three riddles, and if you answer two, you may stay for tea.
The Hatter asks: "Why is a raven like a writing-desk?"
"I give it up. What's the answer?"
"I haven't the slightest idea," said the Hatter. Quite right: in the book nobody knows, not even him. Years later Carroll said it had no answer at all. You win this one by not being fooled!
"Because both have quills."
"Ha! A guess! Guesses are for March. Try again."
"Because both are black."
"Writing-desks are hardly ever black. Try again."
Alice whispers: "The Hatter says his watch is two days wrong. What does his watch tell?"
The day of the month
Yes! It tells the day of the month, not the hour. And it's wrong because the March Hare put butter in it. "It was the BEST butter."
Not this watch: it doesn't tell what o'clock it is. It's always six o'clock here anyway.
No, that would be a very odd watch, even here.
The Cheshire Cat smiles: "I shall vanish now. Find my grin, wherever it is left hanging: five times, before the tea gets cold."
"Well! I've often seen a cat without a grin," thought Alice, "but a grin without a cat!"
The White Rabbit drops his gloves: "I'm late, I'm late! Run with me, through every ring, to the Duchess's!"
"Just in time! Here are my gloves. Thank you, thank you!"
Who wrote Alice's Adventures in Wonderland?
Lewis Carroll (Charles Dodgson)
Hans Christian Andersen
What was Lewis Carroll's day job?
A mathematics teacher at Oxford
What did Alice follow down the hole?
A White Rabbit with a pocket-watch
A talking caterpillar
Who drew the first pictures for Alice in 1865?
Which real girl was the story first told to, on a boat trip in 1862?
Oisín in Tír na nÓg
Irish myth (the Fenian Cycle)
Faerie, on the shore road to the Land of Youth
A white horse's horseshoe
Niamh of the Golden Hair
Niamh of the Golden Hair, a princess of Tír na nÓg, the Land of Youth, who rides a white horse over the sea
I came across the sea for you, son of Fionn. In the Land of Youth no one grows old. Will you ride with me?
Oisín, poet and warrior of the Fianna, son of Fionn mac Cumhaill
I have been in the Land of Youth only three years, I think. Only three years. I would see my father and the Fianna again.
Niamh's white horse
Embarr, Niamh's white horse that gallops over the waves
(The white horse tosses its mane. Its hooves do not quite touch the grass.)
Oisín stands by the white horse. "Niamh says I may go home to Ireland to visit, if I never once set foot on the ground. Help me remember what she told me."
Niamh asks: "What must Oisín never do when he reaches Ireland?"
Get down from the horse and touch the ground
Yes. If his foot touches the earth of Ireland, the years will catch up with him all at once.
He may speak. It is something else. Try again.
Look back at the sea
That is another story (Orpheus!). Try again.
In Ireland Oisín finds strangers, and Fionn's great hall in ruins. Men struggle to lift a great stone. Oisín leans from the saddle to help, and his girth snaps... What happens in the old tale?
He falls to the ground and becomes a very old man: 300 years had passed, not three
That's the story. Time runs differently in the Land of Youth. Old Oisín tells the tales of the Fianna to Saint Patrick, and that is how they were remembered.
He flies back over the sea
Not in the old telling. Try again.
The stone turns into gold
No, but it's a kind thought. Try again.
What does Tír na nÓg mean in Irish?
The Island of Stones
The Kingdom of Night
Who was Oisín's father, leader of the Fianna?
Fionn mac Cumhaill
In the story, how long had Oisín really been away?
Which language were these stories first told in?
Orpheus and Eurydice
Greek myth (Ovid, Virgil)
the Underworld, at the foot of the road up to the light
Orpheus's lyre string
Orpheus, the greatest musician of ancient Greece, who sang his way into the Underworld to bring back his wife
My song moved even the stones and the Furies. Hades has said yes. But there is one condition...
Eurydice, Orpheus's wife, a shade who must follow him up out of the Underworld
I hear his lyre. I will follow, if only he does not look back.
Hades, stern king of the Underworld, fair but unbending
Your music has made the dead weep, singer. Take her. Walk ahead, and do not turn round until you reach the light.
Persephone, queen of the Underworld half the year, kind to Orpheus
Go gently. She walks behind you, quiet as a shadow. Trust that she is there.
Hades: "You may lead her back to the world above. She will follow behind you. If you turn and look at her before you reach the light, she stays here forever."
Walk the road up to the light ahead of you. Do NOT turn round: keep looking forward until you reach the glow. (Turning to look behind you, or turning the view right round, ends it.)

You reach the light without looking back! In the old myth, Orpheus could not bear it and turned at the last moment, and Eurydice slipped back into the shades. Here, this once, she steps out into the sun beside you.
Persephone asks: "Why do you think the gods made the rule 'do not look back'?"
To test whether he could trust without seeing
That's how many people read it: a test of trust and patience. Poets have retold it for over 2,000 years.
Because looking back is bad luck in a game
There's more to it than luck. Think about trust. Try again.
Because the road was narrow
The road was the least of it. Try again.
What instrument did Orpheus play?
Which Roman poet told the story in the Metamorphoses?
Which three-headed dog guarded the Underworld?
In the myth, what went wrong at the very end?
Orpheus looked back
He dropped his lyre
Perseus and Medusa
Greek myth (Ovid, Apollodorus)
the Heavens, at the cloud court of Olympus
A silver sickle charm
Perseus, young hero, son of Zeus and Danaë, sent to bring back the head of Medusa
King Polydectes has sent me to fetch the head of a Gorgon. The gods say they will help me... if I choose their gifts wisely.
Athena, goddess of wisdom, who gives Perseus a polished shield
Never look straight at Medusa. Wisdom is knowing where to look.
Hermes, messenger of the gods, quick and witty, who lends Perseus winged sandals and a curved sword
Fast feet, fast wits! The Gorgons live at the edge of the world. You'll want to fly.
Zeus, king of the gods, Perseus's father
My son goes to face the Gorgon. Watch, and help him, dreamer.
Andromeda, princess of Ethiopia, rescued by Perseus from a sea-monster on his way home
My mother boasted I was lovelier than the sea-nymphs, and the sea sent a monster. If Perseus comes this way...
Athena offers gifts. Which one will let Perseus fight Medusa without being turned to stone?
A polished bronze shield, to see her only as a reflection
Yes. Anyone who looks straight at Medusa's face turns to stone. In the shield's reflection, Perseus could see where she was safely.
Then he could not see her at all! Athena's gift was cleverer. Try again.
Strength alone won't help if he is turned to stone first. Try again.
Hermes asks: "And how will you get to the far edge of the world, where the Gorgons sleep?"
Off you go! Hermes's winged sandals carried Perseus through the air. He also had the cap of darkness (from Hades) to be invisible, and a bag to carry the head.
A chariot pulled by lions
Too slow and too loud for sneaking up on Gorgons. Try again.
It's rather a long way. Try again.
Medusa's two Gorgon sisters are asleep. Walk carefully and gather the five glowing stepping-stars across the clouds, the way Perseus flew, quietly.
You crossed without waking the Gorgons. In the myth Perseus took Medusa's head, and from her sprang Pegasus, the winged horse.
On the way home, Perseus sees Andromeda chained to a rock with a sea-monster coming. What does he do in the myth?
He saves her, and they later marry
Right. And they both became constellations: you can see Perseus and Andromeda in the night sky in autumn.
Not our hero. Try again.
He asks the monster nicely to go away
Polite, but not what happened. Try again.
Medusa was one of the three...
What sprang from Medusa when Perseus defeated her?
Pegasus, the winged horse
Perseus and Andromeda are both names of...
Constellations in the night sky
Which goddess gave Perseus the polished shield?
Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea
the Depths, beside the Nautilus at the reef
A Nautilus brass rivet
Captain Nemo, the proud, mysterious, brilliant captain of the submarine Nautilus, who has left the land behind and loves the sea
Welcome aboard the Nautilus, professor's friend. The sea is everything. It covers seven-tenths of the globe.
Professor Pierre Aronnax, French marine biologist, the narrator, held aboard the Nautilus and amazed by everything he sees
Every fish, every coral, I note it all! What a laboratory this ocean is.
Ned Land, the hot-tempered Canadian master harpooner who wants to escape
A fine boat, sure. But a man needs land under his feet. Keep your eyes open, friend.
Conseil, Aronnax's calm, loyal servant who loves classifying sea creatures
If master pleases, I can tell you the class, order and family of anything that swims past.
Nemo: "Today we walk on the sea floor in our diving suits, to the ruins of a city the sea swallowed long ago. Keep close."
Search the drowned ruins (in the book Nemo shows Aronnax lost Atlantis) and find five carved stones the sea has kept.
Aronnax: "Atlantis! I was walking on its streets!" (A story, of course: no real Atlantis has ever been found.)
A giant squid wraps an arm round the Nautilus! What is the real animal behind the book's monster?
The giant squid, which really lives in the deep ocean
Yes. Giant squid can reach about 12 metres. The first photographs of a live one were only taken in 2004.
The octopus from a fish tank
Far too small. Try again.
Whales actually eat giant squid! Try again.
Nemo asks: "How does the Nautilus make its electricity, deep under the sea?"
From batteries, using sodium taken from seawater
That's Verne's idea. Real submarines of his time barely worked; now submarines run on batteries and even nuclear power.
Fire needs air, and there's none down here. Try again.
Poetic! But no. Try again.
What was Captain Nemo's submarine called?
Jules Verne was from which country?
A league in the title measures...
Distance travelled, not depth
How deep they dived
How fast they went
About how much of the Earth's surface is ocean?
The Little Mermaid
Hans Christian Andersen, 1837
the Depths, by the sea-witch's grotto
A sea-garden flower
the youngest daughter of the sea king in Andersen's story, who longs for the world above and a human soul
My sisters tell me of ships and towns and birds that sing. I have a garden shaped like the sun. Have you ever stood on land?
the little mermaid's wise old grandmother, who knows about the world above
When you are fifteen you may rise up and sit on the rocks in the moonlight and watch the great ships.
the sea witch of Andersen's story, frightening but honest about the terrible price of her bargains
I know what you want. It's stupid of you, but you shall have it, and it will bring you sorrow.
The sea witch offers legs instead of a tail. What price does she ask in Andersen's story?
Her beautiful voice
Yes: the witch takes her voice. And every step on her new feet will feel like walking on knives. Andersen's tale is much sadder than later films.
Far worse than pearls. Try again.
Her grandmother's crown
The grandmother asks: "How does Andersen's story really end?"
She becomes a daughter of the air, a spirit who can earn a soul by doing good
That's Andersen's ending: not wedding bells, but kindness. The statue of the Little Mermaid in Copenhagen has sat on her rock since 1913.
She marries the prince and they live happily ever after
That's a later film's ending, not Andersen's. Try again.
She becomes the new sea witch
Not quite. Try again.
Hans Christian Andersen came from which country?
Where is the famous Little Mermaid statue?
What did the sea witch take in exchange for legs?
Andersen also wrote...
The Call of Cthulhu
the Void, before the carved stone that sends strange dreams
George Gammell Angell, an old professor of ancient languages in Providence who collected strange reports of dreams
Strange dreams, young friend. Artists and poets all over the world, all on the same nights in 1925, dreaming of a sunken city.
Wilcox the sculptor
Henry Wilcox, a nervous young sculptor who carved a strange creature in clay after a dream
I dreamed of great stone cities, slimy and green, and a voice that wasn't a voice. So I made this. I don't know what it is.
Leave it sleeping, and write down what we learned
